title: The stained cloth
hookLine: a dirty cloth won't take the dye; a cleansed mind takes the good (MN 7)
last: BHAYA-BHERAVA — FACE IT WHERE IT FINDS YOU.

cards: Home dyers learn one rule the hard way, usually on a favorite shirt: wash it first. If there's grease or grime in the cotton, the color comes out patchy and dull, however good the dye is, and more dye won't fix it.
You can't cover a stain with color. Take it out, and then the color holds. MN 7 uses this same picture for the mind.

teach.h: A STAINED CLOTH TAKES DYE BADLY.
teach.b: MN 7, the Vatthupama, the simile of the cloth. Suppose a cloth were stained and dirty, the Buddha says, and a dyer dipped it in blue, or yellow, or red, or crimson. It would come out badly dyed, impure in color.
Why? Because the cloth wasn't clean. Dip a clean, bright cloth, and it takes the dye beautifully.
In the same way, when the mind is stained, an unhappy destination can be expected; when the mind is clean, a happy one.
Then he names sixteen stains: covetousness, ill will, anger, revenge, contempt, domineering, envy, stinginess, deceit, fraud, obstinacy, rivalry, conceit, arrogance, vanity and negligence.
It's an old list, and it could describe an ordinary week online.

teach.h: SEE THE STAIN, LET IT GO.
teach.b: The key move is seeing a stain as a stain, and letting it go. Then the cloth is ready. And what color does it take?

Confidence in the Buddha, the teaching and the community. Then the four immeasurables: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, filling the world in every direction. Not dye first and hope it covers.

teach.h: CLEAN FIRST, THEN THE COLOR HOLDS.
teach.b: Clean first; then the color holds.

The Dhammapada has a dyed-cloth verse too, in Max Müller's translation: “He who wishes to put on the yellow dress without having cleansed himself from sin” is not worthy of it, the verse goes on. The robe is the color.

how: In Theravada and other monastic communities, robes are dyed in shades of ochre, saffron or brown, and MN 7's image of washing before dyeing is used to describe clearing the mind's stains before cultivating the immeasurables.

o: a washing ritual before entering a shrine
a dye used to color the robes of monks
a stain or defilement that clouds the mind

games.q: match the pieces of the simile.
p: dips the cloth in blue or crimson

s: the sutta says more dye can cover a stained cloth
a stained cloth comes out badly dyed; it has to be clean first.
envy and conceit are among the sixteen stains
with anger, contempt, stinginess, vanity and the rest.
in MN 7, the clean mind takes on the four immeasurables
loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity, in every direction.

games.q: you're a dyer with a beautiful crimson dye and a stained, dirty cloth. what does the simile say happens when you dip it?
o: the color comes out patchy and impure
games.why: it comes out badly dyed, because the cloth wasn't clean. the mind is the same: see the stains, let them go, and then the good takes.

practice: Pick one stain from the list that you recognize, envy, maybe, or an old grudge, or vanity, and see it plainly, the way you'd hold a shirt up to the light and say: there's the mark.
On each out-breath, loosen your grip on it a little. For the last part of the sit, let one color in: wish one person well.

wordCard.voice: Upakkilesa, stain or defilement. A dirty cloth won't take the dye; a mind washed of its stains takes the good.

orig.note: Pali upakkilesa: defilement, stain; the sutta's word for the sixteen.

carryVoice: Your line: clean cloth takes dye. Sixteen stains, and one good color waiting. Day four hundred seven.

sources.q: He who wishes to put on the yellow dress without having cleansed himself from sin
